reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Endocrine Society
clinicalPearls: The commonest hormone-secreting pituitary tumour; presentation differs by sex, with menstrual disturbance and galactorrhoea in women and reduced libido or erectile dysfunction in men
Because men lack an early hormonal warning sign, they more often present late with large tumours causing mass effect
Hyperprolactinaemia suppresses gonadotrophin secretion, producing hypogonadism, infertility, and reduced bone density over time
Before diagnosing a prolactinoma, exclude other causes of raised prolactin such as pregnancy, hypothyroidism, renal failure, and dopamine-blocking drugs
Stalk compression by any large sellar mass can modestly raise prolactin; very high levels are more specific for a true prolactinoma
In large tumours with only mildly elevated prolactin, laboratory dilution may be needed to exclude the hook effect artefact
Unlike most pituitary tumours, prolactinomas are usually managed medically with dopamine agonists rather than surgery as first line
Dopamine agonist therapy typically lowers prolactin, restores gonadal function, and shrinks tumour volume
reference.pathophysiology: A prolactinoma is a benign lactotroph adenoma of the anterior pituitary that autonomously secretes prolactin. Prolactin is normally under tonic inhibitory control by hypothalamic dopamine, which is why dopamine agonists are effective and dopamine-blocking drugs raise prolactin. Excess prolactin inhibits pulsatile gonadotrophin-releasing hormone secretion, reducing LH and FSH and causing hypogonadism, galactorrhoea, and infertility. Larger tumours (macroadenomas) may compress the optic chiasm and adjacent pituitary tissue, producing visual field defects and hypopituitarism. Non-tumoural hyperprolactinaemia from stalk disconnection, drugs, or systemic disease must be distinguished from a true adenoma.
additionalDifferentials: Physiological hyperprolactinaemia of pregnancy or lactation
Primary hypothyroidism raising prolactin via TRH
Chronic kidney disease reducing prolactin clearance
Stalk-effect hyperprolactinaemia from a non-lactotroph sellar mass
additionalInvestigations: Fasting serum prolactin, repeated if borderline, with sample dilution when a hook effect is suspected
Pregnancy test, thyroid function, and renal function to exclude secondary causes
Review of medications that raise prolactin
Pituitary MRI to characterise adenoma size and suprasellar extension
Assessment of macroprolactin when clinical picture and level are discordant
Visual fields and anterior pituitary hormone panel for macroadenomas
redFlags: Bitemporal visual field loss from chiasmal compression by a macroadenoma
Sudden severe headache with visual or cranial nerve signs suggesting apoplexy
Symptoms and signs of coexisting hypopituitarism, including adrenal insufficiency
Very large invasive tumours threatening vision or requiring urgent decompression
reference.prognosis: Most microprolactinomas respond well to dopamine agonists with normalisation of prolactin, restoration of fertility, and often no significant growth; macroadenomas also usually shrink with medical therapy, and in selected patients treatment can eventually be tapered, though relapse of hyperprolactinaemia is possible.
pitfalls: Diagnosing a prolactinoma without excluding drugs, hypothyroidism, renal failure, and pregnancy
Missing the hook effect and underestimating prolactin in a large tumour, leading to inappropriate surgery
Overlooking macroprolactin as a cause of asymptomatic elevation
Failing to counsel on bone health and fertility implications of chronic hypogonadism
management: Start a dopamine agonist as first-line therapy, usually cabergoline, to normalise prolactin, restore gonadal function and fertility, and shrink the tumour
Reserve transsphenoidal surgery for dopamine-agonist resistance or intolerance, or for acute chiasmal compression or pituitary apoplexy
Monitor response with serial serum prolactin, pituitary MRI and, in macroadenomas, formal visual field testing
Screen for and replace coexisting anterior pituitary hormone deficiencies in macroadenomas, and address hypogonadism-related bone loss with sex steroid replacement
In pregnancy switch to bromocriptine or withdraw treatment as advised and monitor clinically for symptomatic tumour enlargement
Consider echocardiographic surveillance for valvulopathy during prolonged higher-dose cabergoline therapy
Escalate urgently for sudden headache, visual loss or apoplexy, and refer to a pituitary multidisciplinary team for resistant or aggressive tumours
